questions.q: What is PAM, in plain terms?
options: A shared framework that programs like login, sudo, and sshd call into for authentication instead of each implementing it themselves
A graphical password manager built into GNOME
A Linux kernel module that encrypts the filesystem
A replacement for the /etc/passwd file
questions.explain: PAM — Pluggable Authentication Modules — lets authentication logic live in one shared place that every calling program uses.

questions.q: Where does PAM configuration for a given service, such as sudo, actually live?
options: In a file matching the service name under /etc/pam.d/, such as /etc/pam.d/sudo
Inside the sudo binary itself, compiled in
In /etc/shadow, alongside the password hashes
There is no per-service configuration — PAM applies the same rules everywhere with no files
questions.explain: Each service that calls into PAM has its own config file under /etc/pam.d/, read by libpam when that program authenticates.

options: Checks a typed password against the hashed value stored in /etc/shadow
Locks an account after too many failed login attempts
Encrypts the user's home directory
Generates a one-time MFA code
questions.explain: pam_unix.so is the traditional Unix password-check module, verifying a password against its stored hash.

questions.q: In pam_faillock.so's configuration deny=5 unlock_time=900, what happens?
options: The account locks after 5 failed attempts and automatically unlocks after 900 seconds (15 minutes)
The account is permanently disabled after 5 attempts
The user is logged out after 900 seconds of inactivity
900 users can be locked out simultaneously
questions.explain: deny sets the failed-attempt threshold and unlock_time sets how long the resulting lockout lasts, in seconds.

questions.q: Why does adding pam_faillock.so to a shared PAM stack like system-auth protect sudo, ssh, and login all at once?
options: Because all three call into the same shared stack, a module added to that shared config applies to every caller without changing any program's own code
It doesn't — each program would still need its own separate lockout logic
Because sudo, ssh, and login are actually the same program internally
Because pam_faillock.so only works when all three are running simultaneously
questions.explain: That's the core benefit of PAM's design: one policy change in a shared stack reaches every program that includes it.
